content: Albuterol demonstrates a preferential effect on beta-2 adrenergic receptors compared to isoproterenol. Beta-2 adrenergic receptors are predominantly found in bronchial smooth muscle, but they are also present in the human heart at concentrations ranging from 10% to 50%. The exact role of these cardiac beta-2 receptors remains unclear. The pharmacologic effects of beta-adrenergic agonists, including albuterol, are partially mediated by the stimulation of intracellular adenyl cyclase via beta-adrenergic receptors. This enzyme catalyzes the conversion of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cyclic AMP). Elevated cyclic AMP levels are associated with relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle and inhibition of the release of immediate hypersensitivity mediators, particularly from mast cells. Controlled clinical trials have shown that albuterol is more effective than isoproterenol in relaxing bronchial smooth muscle at comparable doses, while producing fewer cardiovascular side effects. Albuterol has a longer duration of action than isoproterenol, regardless of the route of administration. This is because albuterol is not a substrate for cellular uptake processes for catecholamines or for catechol-O-methyltransferase. Studies comparing increasing doses of albuterol and isoproterenol aerosols in both healthy volunteers and asthmatic patients revealed that albuterol is only one-half to one-quarter as active as isoproterenol in increasing heart rate. Similar cardiovascular differences were observed in asthmatic patients. Preclinical studies in rats have shown that albuterol sulfate crosses the blood-brain barrier, achieving brain concentrations approximately 5% of plasma levels. In structures outside the blood-brain barrier, such as the pineal and pituitary glands, albuterol concentrations were found to be 100 times higher than in the whole brain. Studies in laboratory animals (minipigs, rodents, and dogs) have demonstrated the occurrence of cardiac arrhythmias and sudden death, with histologic evidence of myocardial necrosis, when beta-agonists and methylxanthines are administered concurrently. The clinical significance of these findings is unknown. Pharmacokinetic studies indicate that systemic levels of albuterol are low after inhalation of recommended doses due to its gradual absorption from the bronchi. In studies with tritiated albuterol, maximum plasma concentrations occurred within two to four hours. Urinary excretion data suggest that albuterol has an elimination half-life of approximately 3.8 hours. About 72% of the inhaled dose is excreted within 24 hours in the urine, with 28% as unchanged drug and 44% as metabolites. Nonclinical toxicology studies have shown that albuterol sulfate caused a dose-related increase in benign leiomyomas of the mesovarium in a two-year study in Sprague-Dawley rats. This effect was blocked by coadministration of propranolol, a non-selective beta-adrenergic antagonist. However, no evidence of tumorigenicity was observed in an 18-month study in CD-1 mice or a 22-month study in Golden hamsters at significantly higher doses. Albuterol sulfate was not mutagenic in various in vitro and in vivo assays, and reproduction studies in rats showed no evidence of impaired fertility at high oral doses. In controlled clinical trials involving adults with asthma, improvement in pulmonary function was observed within 15 minutes of albuterol administration, with near-maximal improvement occurring within 60 to 90 minutes. Clinically significant improvement generally persisted for three to four hours in most patients, with some showing therapeutic responses lasting up to six hours. Continued effectiveness of albuterol was demonstrated over a 13-week period in these trials. In children aged 4 to 12 years, maximum improvement in pulmonary function occurred within 30 to 60 minutes, with clinically significant improvement observed as early as five minutes in some cases. The majority of pediatric patients maintained significant improvement for two hours, and a subset showed continued improvement for up to four hours. In other clinical studies, two inhalations of albuterol aerosol taken approximately 15 minutes before exercise effectively prevented exercise-induced bronchospasm, as demonstrated by maintaining FEV1 values within 80% of baseline.
